title: Machig Labdrön
hookLine: the Tibetan woman teacher who, tradition says, founded chöd, offering the body to fear

cards: A burial ground at night, high on the Tibetan plateau. Wind, a scatter of bones, a small hand drum in one hand and a bell in the other.
Someone sits down in the one place everyone else walks around, and does it on purpose.
Tradition traces this practice to a woman named Machig Labdrön, a reader of the Perfection of Wisdom sutras who became a teacher with students of her own.
What she taught sounds backward at first: walk toward the thing that frightens you, and offer it a meal.

teach.h: CHÖD: CUTTING THE GRIP OF SELF.
teach.b: First, the name of her practice: chöd, a Tibetan word meaning to cut. What gets cut is not a person, and not really a demon.
In her teaching, the true demon is the grip of the self, the habit of clutching at me and mine, and fear is where that grip shows itself most plainly. Second, the method.

teach.h: OFFER THE BODY TO EVERY HUNGRY BEING.
teach.b: In the visualization, the practitioner imagines leaving the body behind and offering it as food and nectar to every hungry being, the gentle guests and the frightening ones alike. Nothing is held back.
The point is not to act brave. It is to stop guarding the very thing fear is trying to protect. Third, the root.

teach.h: THE PERFECTION OF WISDOM, IN THE DARK.
teach.b: Machig's practice rests on the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, which teach that nothing has a separate, solid self.
Chöd takes that teaching off the page and into the dark: if there is no solid self, whatever the demon eats was never really owned.
Her life stories describe a teacher who had a family, raised children, and gathered students, and tradition says her teaching even traveled from Tibet back to India, a stream flowing the other way.
Chöd is still practiced in Tibetan Buddhism, often with the drum and bell, and it is traditionally received from a teacher after preparation. It is not a dare.
It is generosity, aimed at the thing you'd rather run from.

how: Chöd is practiced in Tibetan Buddhist communities, usually after receiving it from a teacher, with chanted liturgy, a hand drum and bell, and a visualized offering of the body; some practitioners do it in lonely or frightening places.

o: a Tibetan teacher who taught offering yourself to fear
an Indian queen who built Tibet's first temple
a Chinese nun who carried sutras across the desert

p: to cut: the grip of self
the body, to every hungry being

s: chöd is a ritual for fighting demons
in her teaching, the real demon is the grip of the self, and the practice offers rather than fights.
chöd rests on the Perfection of Wisdom sutras
it takes their teaching of no solid self into the dark.

games.q: night in a burial ground. you sit down to practice, and fear rises in your chest. what does chöd ask of you?
o: get up and find a lamp
fight the fear until it leaves
games.why: chöd turns toward the fear and offers, in visualization, the very body fear wants to protect.

practice: Bring to mind one small fear, not the biggest one, a phone call you keep putting off or a worry about a bill, and notice where it shows up in the body.

Don't push it away, and don't feed the story; turn toward it the way you'd turn toward a guest at the door, letting your hands open a little on each out-breath. If it grows too big, come back to the breath alone.

wordCard.voice: Machig Labdrön. The Tibetan teacher whom tradition credits with chöd, cutting the grip of self by offering it to fear. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan chöd (written gcod): to cut. what is cut is the grip of the self.

carryVoice: Your line: offer it to fear. Whatever it eats was never really yours to guard. Day nine hundred seventy-seven, done.
